faq.answer: No. Housing arrangements, sensory access, remote work, confidentiality, family roles, study needs, and ordinary preference can all make private space useful without establishing subtype.
faq.question: Does wanting a private room prove self-preservation Type Five?

faq.answer: Compare behavior after resources, housing, and workload become reliably sufficient. If protection decreases with stable access, the material constraint explains more than a subtype label.
faq.question: How can actual scarcity be separated from this hypothesis?

faq.answer: Flexible sharing when access is reliable, comfortable interruption, and rapid relaxation of limits after a constraint ends should all reduce confidence in the subtype account.
faq.question: What counterexample weakens the resource-boundary hypothesis?

sections.body_md: Within a Type Five hypothesis, self-preservation may emphasize maintaining a workable base with sufficient space, supplies, time, and low-demand access. This remains secondary and must be tested against actual constraints.
sections.title: State the tradition as a testable secondary idea

sections.body_md: Observe two similar weeks with the same workload: one with secure housing and predictable access, another with scarcity or interruption. Ask whether boundary protection persists after resources and demands become stable.
sections.title: Compare identical resources under different constraints

sections.body_md: The self-preservation label organizes observations about resource and boundary attention; it is not evidence about bodily mechanisms, neurological systems, or a universal biological category.
sections.title: Avoid bodily-mechanism claims

sections.body_md: A person may host others, lead a public project, or share resources while still using clear time and space limits. Visible generosity neither proves nor disproves the hypothesis; compare the boundary negotiation.
sections.title: Allow visible participation beside protected capacity

sections.body_md: Housing insecurity, disability access, chronic workload, caregiving, poverty, migration, sensory needs, and unsafe environments can make space or supplies urgent. These conditions deserve direct support, not a subtype interpretation.
sections.title: Audit material and access conditions first

sections.body_md: Confidence should fall when secure resources lead to easy sharing, interruptions are handled without prolonged retreat, low-demand routines are not preferred, or boundaries shift readily after a specific constraint ends.
sections.title: Use stable access and flexible sharing as challenges

sections.body_md: One measure and sample cannot establish universal subtype ontology or cross-cultural equivalence. Treat resource patterns as local observations, preserve alternatives, and require human review before any later use.
sections.title: Keep the construct instrument-specific and revisable

sections.body_md:
Duration: 5

Context: Across five days, compare one resource decision, one interruption, and one shared-space event.

Observable signal: Record available supplies, housing security, access needs, workload, caregiving duty, stated boundary, and later adjustment.

Page-specific signal: Hold the task constant while comparing a secure-resource period with a constrained-resource period.

Alternative explanation: Check scarcity, housing, disability access, remote work, confidentiality, sensory demand, and current safety.

Reflection prompt: Identify whether a boundary relaxes when the named constraint ends and revise the subtype hypothesis.

seo.description: Type Five self-preservation is a traditional subtype hypothesis about attention to space, resources, low-demand arrangements, and protecting usable capacity. A private room, stocked supplies, or reduced contact does not establish subtype because scarcity, housing, disability access, caregiving, remote work, confidentiality, and safety may explain the same choices.
seo.title: Type Five self-preservation: a space and resource boundary hypothesis
